77b98a1fcc32d5af: SYDNEY: Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about US$2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.
From Singapore and Shanghai to London and Berlin, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days.

Competitors such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones.
It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary".
Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online.
In Sydney, which was the first Apple store to sell the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 (US$2,734) for a 512GB Duo.

In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to six straight quarters of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices.
Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6am for Apple's first foldable.
"I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.
Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models.
Others were resellers.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 (US$2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked.
Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain.
"Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said.
Mixed reviews

Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.
But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers.
They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers.

"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the US$2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."
In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.

"I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices."
TOUGH TO FIND
Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.
IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.
"Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo.
"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.
ff55915616e3a5c5: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I.

Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as "Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop." In the podcast Pivot to AI, podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: "This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI."

I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous.

I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse, which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place.

Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them.

All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful.

Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today.

In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception.

Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to "deprecate the Assisted-by Tag." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions.

That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool."

Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so.

As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe: "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming.

Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real."

True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers.

Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides "tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it."

By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers.

In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question."

He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself."
It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®
4d9ebe56a9774973: Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it.

As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. This has enabled Ukraine to maintain vital communications for both civilian purposes and military operations—and has also expanded the Ukrainian military’s capability to remotely control or provide guidance to drones used in both air defense against Russian attacks and for striking back at Russian targets.

“Starlink currently offers some of the best satellite coverage available, with virtually no competitors when you consider the combination of cost, availability, and ease of use,” according to the head of hardware R&D at the Ukrainian defense company BlueBird Tech, who provided comments to Ars anonymously for security reasons. “In practical terms, the main limitation is the need to position the antenna so it can receive signals from the satellites.”

86d3f2c86706447f: Peacock series Crystal Lake doesn’t feel like a Friday the 13th movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original Friday the 13th movie but avoids major Crystal Lake spoilers.)

Instead, Crystal Lake strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory, while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son, Jason.

Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans, who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth.
9a0af2f9075d0a33: BENGALURU: The combined China-India-Brazil market for weight-loss drugs could grow to US$22 billion by 2035 from US$6.6 billion currently, J.P. Morgan estimated, as improving affordability and broader access drive adoption in largely untapped patient populations.
The addressable market could grow at an annual rate of 15% through 2035, J.P. Morgan analysts led by Yang Huang said in a note on Friday, given the countries' large diabetes and obesity burdens.
GLP-1 drugs, such as Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound, have become some of the most sought-after medicines for weight-loss and diabetes treatment globally.

China and India are home to some of the world's largest diabetes patient populations, accounting for more than 25% and 15% of global diagnosed cases, respectively, while about 12% of Brazilian adults have diabetes, according to J.P. Morgan.
The three countries also face a growing obesity burden. China's overweight and obese population could exceed 65% by 2030, while India's adult obesity rate is projected to reach 11% by 2035.
"GLP-1 is transitioning from a developed-market growth theme to a broader global access story..." the analysts said.
"With patent cliffs, generic launches and policy-engineered price cuts now improving GLP-1 affordability, the three markets are converging on the same destination."
GLP-1's uptake in many emerging markets has remained low due to affordability concerns. Penetration is below 0.1% in China and under 0.2% in India, versus 4%-5% in the US, according to the note.
While Brazil is currently the largest of the three markets, obesity-drug penetration is projected to reach only 7%-8% of its obese population by 2035, compared with about 30% in the US.

J.P. Morgan expects China to overtake Brazil by 2027, with its market reaching US$13.7 billion by 2035, versus US$8 billion for Brazil, supported by its large diabetes burden and wider reimbursement for GLP-1 therapies.

For India, the smallest of the three markets, conservative attitudes toward GLP-1 drugs, alongside affordability concerns, remain key barriers to adoption, J.P. Morgan said, as hesitancy around injectables and slow-shifting cultural attitudes persist.
The brokerage highlighted China's Innovent, Divi's Laboratories and Torrent Pharmaceuticals in India, and Brazil's RD Saude as its key stocks to play the GLP-1 growth theme.

6a1f84e9ac5097f9: PARIS: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is en route to New York after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Moscow in early October, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.
The tanker Agioi Fanendes, sailing under the Maltese flag, was located off Helsinki on Friday and indicated "New York" as its destination via its AIS transponder signal.
It loaded nearly 300,000 barrels of diesel at the Russian oil terminal of Primorsk, according to Kpler.
It left Primorsk on the night of Oct 22 to 23 and is expected to arrive on the US East Coast around Nov 7.

On Wednesday, Russian news agencies cited Russian Deputy Prime Minister for Energy Alexander Novak saying the first shipment of Russian diesel bound for the United States would depart the following day.
In early October, Trump announced an agreement between Washington and Moscow for the delivery of Russian diesel to the US market, in the process lifting sanctions against Russia.

The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm legislative elections on Nov 3 and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies, and even from within Trump's Republican Party.
93a6b96277e80384: DUBAI, Oct 23 — UAE national airline Etihad has extended until November 5 its suspension of flights to Riyadh and Dammam in Saudi Arabia, targeted by strikes from Yemen’s Houthis.
Etihad had suspended its service to Riyadh on October 12, two days after a deadly attack on a passenger terminal killed 13 people.
In a statement yesterday, Etihad specified that flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam would remain suspended due to “operational disruptions”.
On Wednesday evening, two people were killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport.
The airport, however, reopened the following day, while the capital’s airport remains closed.
Etihad added that it would operate only daytime flights to the western city of Jeddah, with night flights cancelled until November 5.
In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure including oil facilities and airports have reached a scale unprecedented since the start of the conflict in Yemen in 2014. — AFP
affe2185b1f2b488: Working in the same place for what feels like millennia can have its benefits, however working for the same place for what seems like millennia carrying over all the benefits of your original contract can be even better than that.

Some of those benefits are, admittedly, useless to me. I'm unlikely to avail myself of the Company-reimbursed landline (that all on-call personnel are entitled to), and I won't be needing the 2400bps modem or the VT100 for after hours support. The one month pregnancy leave is also off the cards.

What is in play, however, as the PFY has recently discovered, is accumulated sick leave. It appears that we've been racking up two weeks a year to a point that I now have sufficient sick leave to safely get leprosy.
Obviously, I'm not going to exercise that particular option, but both the PFY and I have been considering roads not taken in recent times...
"Ahh... Just, um, following up on your recent, uh, illnesses." The Boss asks uneasily.
"Oh yes?" I ask.
"This, uh, acute bronchitis a few Fridays back."
"Oh yeah, it was terrible," I lie. "Hacking cough, not pleasant at all. I was wheezing like a coal-fired Trabant."
"And that particular illness lasted... a single day?"
"Apparently," I say. "All good now though."
"And Stephen. He had acute... otitis media around the same time."
"The ear thing?" I respond. "Yes, apparently it really affected his balance."
"Okay, fair enough. But then you had acute sinusitis on the Monday? And Stephen had asthma on the Tuesday?"
"Yes, that sounds about right." I nod.
"Then.. Back spasms for you last Friday and campylobacter for Stephen on Monday?"

"I blame myself. I carried a large Vindaloo banquet for six back to work on the Wednesday night. The PFY took the leftovers back home for dinner following day. He's never been great with food hygiene."
"And then I see fibromyalgia for you and food poisoning for Stephen?"
"Yeah, like I said, he's not that great with food hygiene. He tends to follow the five minute rule."
"Hmm. And is there any reason why you seem to be getting sick in... uh... alphabetical order?" the Boss asks.
"It's as much a mystery to you as to me," I admit, making a mental note to vary things a bit. "Illness seems to be attracted to us like a hippy to a salt lamp."
"And, uh, no medical certificate for any of these illnesses?" the Boss enquires.
"I checked with Claude, and he told me that according to my contract I'd only need a med cert for a three-or-more-days illness."
"You have been ill for more than three days. Just yesterday you had conjunctivitis."
"Firstly, I believe it's contiguous sick days, and secondly, the conjunctivitis was so bad it would have been irresponsible to drive to the doctor..."
"And yet your eyesight was sufficient for you to type in questions to Claude?" the Boss asks, astutely.
"Oh no, I spoke to Claude."
It's a bit early to be calling check-mate at this stage, but I have to admit to feeling smug.
"The actual wording of your contract indicates that the conditions can be varied by written notice," the Boss points out.
"And I take it you've written a notice?" I ask, noticing a folded page in the Boss' hand.
The Boss hands the paper to me, still warm from the printer.
"You'll note that it's in writing, signed and dated," the Boss points out.
"Well that's me told," I say, feeling a little like I'll have a dental problem tomorrow.
...two days later...
"And so I'm just after your med cert for your, er, dental abscess," the Boss asks, skipping the niceties.

"Oh yes, right. I spoke to Claude, and he looked over my contract again. Apparently he says that giving me written notice is (a) not retrospective, and that I probably already had the dental issue before you gave me written notice, but also (b) written notice can only vary the contract by mutual agreement."
"And I take it you don't agree?" the Boss asks.
"Claude says I don't. But I got a medical opinion anyway."
… two minutes later..
"An email, apparently from Claude, saying it definitely sounds like you have an abscess is NOT a medical certificate."
"But Claude's a medical expert. He's got access to a vast database of medical information on the web."
"That doesn't count," the Boss snaps.
"Claude says it does," I counter.
"Oh, so Claude's a lawyer as well then?" the Boss snaps sarcastically.
"No, Claude's our new cleaner. Hell of a nice bloke. He suggested I talk to AI about my contract and everything."
"And?"
"Oh. It agrees with Claude. Oh, and it pointed out that apparently you owe Stephen and me a landline, a 2400 baud modem and a VT100 terminal."
"And I take it that's Stephen's opinion as well?"
"I'm not sure. I'll know when he gets back from gastroenteritis tomorrow. Honestly, that guy needs to use a fridge..." ®

a221aaf937100eca: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — Bursa Malaysia ended the week on a flattish note, although the benchmark index managed to finish marginally higher as selective buying in index heavyweights helped offset cautious sentiment ahead of the weekend, said an analyst.
At 5pm, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) gained 3.42 points or 0.21 per cent to end at its intraday high of 1,611.56 from yesterday’s close of 1,608.14.
The index, which opened 0.51 of a point lower at 1,607.63, hit an intraday low of 1,604.38 during the mid-morning trading session.
On the broader market, decliners and gainers were almost even at 529 to 528, while 532 counters were unchanged, 1,312 untraded and 16 suspended.
Turnover improved to 3.18 billion units worth RM2.47 billion from Thursday’s 2.89 billion units worth RM2.69 billion.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said sentiment remained fragile following Wall Street’s technology-led correction, with the Nasdaq falling 2.6 per cent overnight amid renewed concerns over the financing and profitability of AI (artificial intelligence) investments.
“As for the local bourse, we view the FBM KLCI’s ability to hold above 1,600 as an encouraging sign, although buying conviction remains modest,” he told Bernama.

Among heavyweights, Maybank jumped nine sen to RM10.06, Public Bank advanced four sen to RM4.75, TNB increased six sen to RM13.30, CIMB was flat at RM7.15, and IHH Healthcare eased nine sen to RM7.90.

Of the active stocks, Zetrix AI gained 2.5 sen to 7.5 sen, Top Glove improved four sen to 92 sen, Ni Hsin went up three sen to 49 sen, VS Industry was flat at 33 sen, and CBH Engineering shed four sen to 90.5 sen.

Among the top gainers, Nestle rose 58 sen to RM89.54, Kuala Lumpur Kepong expanded by 22 sen to RM20.52, Hong Leong Industries put on 18 sen to RM16.30, and Petronas Chemicals garnered 16 sen to RM4.65.

The top losers included Malaysian Pacific Industries and Hong Leong Bank which trimmed 30 sen each to RM40.00 and RM21.20, respectively, while Press Metal gave up 21 sen to RM6.73, and Genting Plantations shaved off 18 sen to RM5.11.

On the index board, the FBM Mid 70 Index strengthened by 51.96 points to 17,170.33, the FBM Emas Shariah Index rose 11.59 points to 11,943.57, the FBM Emas Index went up 28.95 points to 11,993.45, the FBM Top 100 Index was 27.78 points higher at 11,797.61, and the FBM ACE Index climbed 22.64 points to 5,346.14.

Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index eased 0.05 of a point to 175.40, the Energy Index firmed 2.87 points to 834.67, the Plantation Index garnered 14.80 points to 8,677.48, and the Financial Services Index gained 49.32 points to 18,654.32.
The Main Market volume expanded to 1.69 billion units worth RM2.18 billion from 1.41 billion units worth RM2.37 billion yesterday.
Warrants turnover increased to 1.05 billion units worth RM135.55 million against 941.91 million units worth RM115.13 million yesterday.

16586bf0ec20cfea: DUBAI: UAE national airline Etihad has extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh and Dammam in Saudi Arabia until Nov 5, targeted by strikes from Yemen's Houthis.
Etihad had suspended its service to Riyadh on Oct 12, two days after a deadly attack on a passenger terminal killed 13 people.
In a statement on Thursday, Etihad specified that flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam would remain suspended due to "operational disruptions".
On Wednesday evening, two people were killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport.
The airport, however, reopened the following day, while the capital's airport remains closed.
Etihad added that it would operate only daytime flights to the western city of Jeddah, with night flights cancelled until Nov 5.
In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, have reached a scale unprecedented since the start of the conflict in Yemen in 2014.
423350242b97fb0d: NEW DELHI: Subscriptions for Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's first IPO in two decades surged further on the final day of bidding on Friday, as investors bet on Jio Platforms' US$3.2 billion offering to tap into the nation's telecom and digital sector.

Jio's IPO, India's largest ever, is being closely watched as a test of investor appetite for large listings at a time when AI-linked stocks are facing increased scrutiny. The company, whose mobile network serves more than 500 million users, is launching its IPO during the auspicious Hindu festive season.

Public subscriptions for the IPO crossed 10 times the shares on offer by Friday, driven by strong demand from institutional and retail investors, employees and shareholders. Assuming bids were largely placed at the top end of the 1,119-rupee price band, total demand has now exceeded US$24.5 billion.

That's on top of so-called anchor investors like the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, BlackRock and Fidelity that bid for their exclusively reserved quota on Monday. Their reserved US$854 million worth of shares received bids of over $25 billion.
"This is a Reliance IPO after a long time, which is triggering a lot of exuberance and euphoria for the stock," said Kranthi Bathini, equity strategist at WealthMills Securities.

The IPO values Jio Platforms at up to US$108.3 billion, potentially making it one of India's biggest companies by market capitalisation when trading starts ​on Oct 28. It counts Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google among its investors, and is led by Ambani's eldest son, Akash Ambani.
The IPO got off to an unusually rapid start on Wednesday when the offering was fully subscribed within two hours of opening.
That contrasts with most Indian IPOs, where books typically build gradually and institutional investors often wait until the final hours to place bids.

Jio is part of Ambani's Reliance Industries, a company often seen by Indian investors as a long-term wealth generator. Reliance shares have returned around 900% since 2006, beating the benchmark Nifty index's 685% return, LSEG data shows.

Jio's telecoms business was launched in 2016 and disrupted the market by offering free voice and data, hitting rivals Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea. Today, on the ​basis of customers in a single country, Jio's 500 million-plus users are second only to China Mobile's 600941.SS.

As of Friday, the institutional portion of the IPO was subscribed 26.5 times, underscoring strong demand from large investors. The retail tranche was covered 2.3 times, while bids for the employee and existing Reliance shareholder quotas reached 2.7 and 6.6 times the shares on offer, respectively, exchange data showed.

Reliance was founded by Dhirubhai Ambani, Akash Ambani's grandfather, who cultivated a vast retail investor base through mass shareholder gatherings in Mumbai in the 1980s. On its website, the conglomerate says its 1977 listing helped popularise equity investing in India, "ushering the equity cult" in the country.

e3871f5c44767438: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure.

The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running.

According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology.

The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause.

Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage.

Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security.
The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands.
Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking.

In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes.

"The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray.

The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act.

It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic.

Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates.

And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states.
None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed.

Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

6d8b967bcbddd151: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.
a915ec71e2287e6d: Today's victim of the bork fairy is a claw machine that even Android seems to have rejected for its alleged unfairness. And Google, as we all know, is all about fairness.

Eagle-eyed Register reader Scott spotted the stricken machine in an arcade adjacent to a roller rink, a place our reader visited with a friend and described as "something my currently bruised body reminds me I hadn't done for about 20 years."
We assume they were talking about roller-skating, and not the exertions of accompanying their pal.

The machine itself is a recent iteration of the infamous claw machine, which has spent a century emptying players' pockets in exchange for frustration and the very occasional reward of tat. Infamously, the devices are sometimes rigged so the claw's strength varies between turns, and in several parts of the world, gambling laws cover the machines.

However, the only gambling to be done here is on whether or not Android will boot. Like so many players in the past, the machine has lost this bet, and an Android Recovery Console is on show. We're not sure who lennie022 is – perhaps a user or perhaps some corporate account – but the words "release-keys" probably don't belong on top of the device. They're unlikely to entice any everyday players to part with cash.

The usual recovery menu is hidden thanks to the dimensions of the screen. If something like this comes up on a mobile device, the volume up and down buttons tend to be used for navigation. In this case, the joystick is presumably the only I/O method, and the selected option would be pot-luck. Which, we guess, is the whole point.

More discreet is the screen below the machine which, rather than encourage a player to grip the sweaty handle, is now plaintively asking for some removable storage (we've seen enough electronic gizmos to know what those pictograms mean) on a blue background that would bring a tear to the eye of many a Microsoft engineer.

In fact, something that looks a bit like a blue screen of death and a borked Android? Perhaps this combination would lure an engineer to the controls… Sure, there's no obvious place to stick removable storage or attach a keyboard. But a waggle of the joystick couldn't hurt, could it? Perhaps one more?
Dammit. Now we're restarting Android, when all we wanted was that pink bunny. ®
9e02525728baf1c4: The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has been entrusted with stewardship of four additional AI projects in the hope of broadening the set of vendor-neutral tools for making AI agents.

The AAIF was founded in December 2025 under the auspices of the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral organization for the benefit of AI companies more interested in riding a tide that lifts all boats than making waves.
It launched with three projects under its supervision: Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md. With the four new adoptees, there are now 10 projects sheltering under the AAIF's wings.
The donor organizations – Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face, and OpenAI – have handed over control of OpenSandbox, Agent Skills, OpenEnv, and Open Responses respectively.

Each of these projects provides functions that developers of AI agents – which typically combine models, tools, and a task loop – may find helpful. And having a more or less agreed-upon blueprint for implementation tends to make deployment easier and more predictable, at least until your AI agent unexpectedly ransacks some third-party organization.

OpenSandbox provides a way to constrain or sandbox the capabilities of AI agents using various client SDKs, tools, protocols, lifecycle hooks, container runtimes, and assorted in-sandbox execution components.
Agent Skills outlines a format for text descriptions that guide AI agents through specified tasks more effectively. It provides context that helps agents accomplish their goals.
"We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral," said Anthropic, an AAIF co-founder, in a blog post.
OpenEnv offers a containerized service for creating reinforcement learning environments that can be built without much trouble, can interoperate, and can scale to meet demanding testing.

And Open Responses is an open API specification for building LLM interfaces that can work with different model providers. It standardizes common request and response formats, streaming events, and tool invocation patterns.

The AAIF's nurturing of these technical specs has attracted considerable interest from companies convinced that there's a future in AI agents. The organization has surpassed 300 members in less than a year, with 60 coming on board this quarter, including Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr as Gold Members.

This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries. Axios is reporting that US banks have become concerned that AI agents are interacting with customer accounts without bank authorization (though not necessarily without customer authorization). ®

3ad16c876a13b12b: Energy can be hard to find on Friday mornings, which is why The Register uses them to offer a fresh instalment of On Call – the reader-contributed column that shares your hopefully empowering tech support stories.

This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Lachlan,” who told us he once did tech support for a senior exec who had a side hustle writing essays for Japanese university students attending UK universities.
The exec asked Lachlan for help diagnosing a sudden inability to send or receive email, an obvious hindrance to the side hustle.
This story took place in the dialup age, so Lachlan sensibly assumed that the exec’s modem was misbehaving.
“I checked the network settings, nothing wrong there,” he told On Call. Next, he checked the cables, and if the line the modem used had a dial tone. Again, all was well.

“At this point I decided to make sure the device was correctly installed in Windows Device Manager,” Lachlan wrote. “I had a lot of experience in the dark arts of serial communications and there was an option in the advanced settings in Device Manager to send a series of low level AT commands to the modem, which would return responses.”
He ran the tests, and Windows reported that the modem was in the pink of health.
With all that done, Lachlan decided the time had come to replace the modem.

“When I opened the PC, I got a faint whiff of that unmistakable scorched PCB smell,” he wrote. “By looking at the modem you couldn’t normally see if any of the chips were faulty. In this case there was a black soot mark in the shape of the voltage regulator chip which sits between the phone line and the sensitive chips on the modem.”

“This was to protect the device from the 70V line voltage BT used to create a phone connection,” he explained. “However, in this instance the chip had been vaporized. That wasn’t just a slight over voltage – this was way higher.”
Lachlan asked the exec when his email had stopped working, and if he could recall any recent electrical storms.
He replied by saying his email stopped working while he watched a really impressive display of lightning.
“That voltage regulator chip sacrificed itself for the greater good,” Lachlan wrote.

Has Windows failed to find an obvious fault? Or has lightning lightened your load? In either case, click here to send your story to On Call so we can electrify your fellow readers on a future Friday. ®

690aea53d2bd1733: Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems.  To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas. Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation?  A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective.  In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight.  One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks. Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening. But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form.  Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today? A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers. One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed. Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI? A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer. Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently. But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there. Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development?  A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.
291f0719d1e3f06f: "Malaysians asked to remove haze, government asking to remove Waze". Satu lagi berbunyi, "ask government to settle haze, they got rid of Waze". Tak tahu siapa yang mencipta ungkapan itu tetapi dia memang creative buat lawak sinis.

Ada rhyme 'haze' dengan 'Waze'. Kata-kata itu sudah mendapat tempat di pelbagai platform media sosial. Saya sendiri tersenyum lebar membacanya. Ini susulan tindakan kerajaan melarang penjawat awam menggunakan aplikasi navigasi Waze berkuat kuasa serta-merta. Walaupun larangan membabitkan hanya kakitangan kerajaan, orang ramai turut digalakkan berhenti guna Waze.
Oleh kerana jerebu masih bersama kita, terciptalah jenaka sinis 'haze' dan 'waze' yang disebut tadi. Namun jika diambil kira alasan kerajaan, this is no laughing matter.

Kata Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim, tindakan diambil bagi melindungi maklumat kerajaan dan data peribadi pengguna yakni penjawat awam daripada ancaman penyalahgunaan oleh rejim Israel. Keputusan dibuat PMX dengan mengambil kira kedudukan Waze Mobile Ltd sebagai pengawal data pengguna yang diperbadankan dan beroperasi di bawah undang-undang Israel.

Berkata pula Menteri Digital Gobind Singh Deo, "jika melihat dokumen perjanjian (sebelum mengaktifkan aplikasi) kita bersetuju dengan syarat-syarat tertentu iaitu di bawah bidang kuasa undang-undang Israel dan itu menjadi satu masalah kepada kita."

Majlis Keselamatan Negara pula kata tiada kompromi terhadap sebarang risiko keselamatan melibatkan Israel. Reaksi Waze ialah menafikan aplikasinya mengumpulkan maklumat sensitif kerajaan atau membenarkan pihak ketiga mengeksplotasi data peribadi pengguna. Penafian ini memang dijangkakan.
Larangan kerajaan stands. Ketua Pengarah MKN Raja Nushirwan Zainal Abidin berkata penjawat awam yang melanggar arahan boleh dikenakan tindakan tatatertib.

Saya percaya ramai dalam kalangan ribuan penjawat awam menggunakan Waze. Yang membingungkan saya bagaimana mahu memastikan semua yang menggunakan Waze mematuhi arahan. Adakah setiap penjawat awam akan diperiksa seorang demi seorang? Mengambil kira bilangan kakitangan awam yang guna Waze, pelaksanaan arahan tentunya bukan mudah.
Kata MKN, "dari segi pelaksanaan arahan ada caranya tetapi secara umum kita serahkan kepada ketua jabatan masing-masing". That is not saying much.
Oleh kerana jutaan rakyat menggunakan Waze tentunya larangan kerajaan menarik perhatian ramai.

Pertanyaan ramai ialah why now? Mungkinkah berdasarkan informasi terkini? Jika penggunaan Waze mengancam keselamatan negara dan diri sendri apa lagi yang mengancam ialah Israel, mengapa larangan tidak menyeluruh dan membabitkan semua rakyat, meskipun saya akui ini akan menyebabkan kesulitan.

Menurut Raja Nushirwan, kerajaan mengambil pendekatan berfasa berteraskan pendidikan awam demi mengimbangi tuntutan keselamatan dan kebebasan memilih rakyat. Maka sekarang eloklah kita tunggu 'pendidikan awam' yang beliau katakan. Dalam bentuk apa agaknya ia akan disalurkan kepada rakyat?
"Dengan cara yang kita ambil ini kita serahkan kepada rakyat Malaysia untuk memilih secara sendiri," kata beliau. Terima kasih. Rakyat lain ada pilihan sendiri, tidak seperti penjawat awam.

Menurut Anwar, kerajaan menggalakkan orang ramai untuk menggunakan aplikasi tempatan, TuJu, yang dibangunkan oleh Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia sebagai alternatif bagi keperluan navigasi jalan raya. Jujur saya kata saya tidak tahu akan kewujudan TuJu. Pun begitu semasa menonton Buletin Utama tiga malam lalu, beberapa warganegara yang sudah lama menggunakan TuJu rata-rata puas hati dengan prestasi aplikasi itu.
Apabila Anwar mencadangkan orang ramai guna TuJu, ramai menyambut saranan beliau. Ada lonjakan ketara jumlah pengguna TuJu selepas PMX mengesyorkan pengunaannya. That’s on the upside.

On the downside tercetus gangguan teknikal yang menjejaskan perisian navigasi TuJu. Kata Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia ia sudah bekerjasama dengan penyedia aplikasi, Prosignal Consortium, untuk mengenal pasti punca gangguan, memulihkan kestabilan sistem serta meningkatkan kapasiti aplikasi bagi menampung jumlah pengguna yang semakin bertambah.

Bercakap mengenai penyedia aplikasi TuJu, macam-macam spekulasi dalam kalangan orang ramai yang saya tidak cadang menghuraikan, sekadar menyatakan memang biasa apabila kerajaan recommend sesuatu perkara, syarikat yang mengendalikannya akan diletak di bawah mikroskop. Kadangkala ada spekulasi betul dan ada yang bohong.

Apapun if there's anything good to come out of this Waze issue, it is proof that Malaysia atau lebih tepat rakyat boleh mencipta aplikasi membanggakan. Jika tidak lebih baik, ia setanding Waze. Semakin ramai kenal TuJu maka cepatlah atasi kesulitan.

a52a4b92f90e0388: In a matter of just over a month, a perfect storm has pushed Zetrix AI Bhd to the precipice of corporate oblivion. In the process, the digital services firm’s share price has crashed by over 90% and its market capitalisation has plummeted by over RM5 billion.

The collapse of its shares started on Aug 27 when it opened at 66 sen, with the company valued at about RM5.33 billion. By the end of the day, the company formerly known as My EG Services Bhd had fallen nearly 10% to 59.5 sen.
The next day, the dam broke when the shares suffered a intraday plunge of 50.4% to close at 29.5 sen, erasing RM2.4 billion from its market value.

The monumental collapse was attributed to speculation linking it with the corruption case of former human resources minister M Saravanan as well as forced selling of the shares of its co-founder and group managing director Wong Thean Soon.

Things got progressively worse with the share price falling like a rock as the bad news piled up. On Oct 5, the Road Transport Department (JPJ) suspended Zetrix and its subsidiary MyEG Sdn Bhd as collection agents over unremitted government revenue.
Transport minister Loke Siew Fook then dropped the bombshell that Zetrix failed to remit RM314 million in collected government revenues.
This prompted the police to open an investigation into the matter, with the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) also jumping into the fray.
The troubles afflicting Zetrix put it firmly in the crosshairs of rating agencies. On Oct 18, 2026, MARC Ratings downgraded its RM2 billion sukuk (Islamic bonds) programme rating to BB+IS from AA-IS.
The stock then tumbled on news of a potential covenant breach looming over the sukuk programme. Under its trust deed, Wong is required to remain Zetrix’s single largest shareholder.

However, his stake has been slashed to just 1.84% currently from nearly 30% following forced share sales by banks triggered by margin calls. The sukuk trustee has given Zetrix until Oct 22 to remedy the issue, which seems highly unlikely given Wong is no longer a substantial shareholder.

This means it needs to seek sukuk holders’ approval for a waiver if the breach is not resolved by then. Without a waiver, the breach could trigger early repayment of the RM2 billion principal as well as RM164.5 million in future coupon payments.
Any default of the sukuk will trigger a Practice Note 17 (PN17) classification. That would be catastrophic for Zetrix.
To aggravate matters, the company announced it was withdrawing its first interim dividend of 0.25 sen per share (amounting to RM19.7 million) for FY2026 declared two months ago to “conserve cash”.

In the face of all the bad press, Zetrix’s share price hit an intraday low of 5 sen last Friday (Oct 16), its lowest level in over 14 years, valuing the company at RM404 million. The stock is within touching distance of its all-time low price of 3.5 sen, which was reached in 2008.
Zetrix’s paradox
Ironically, Zetrix should be trading nearer to its all-time high than its record low, based on its financial results.
For the year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025), its net profit hit RM883.85 million, a 24.9% rise from the previous year, while revenue jumped 31.3% to RM1.34 billion.
Just two days before Zetrix’s selloff started end-August, MBSB Research forecast it would hit RM1.1 billion in core earnings for FY2026.
MBSB noted Zetrix’s normalised earnings for the first half of 2026 jumped 38.9% to RM540.7 million, and was on track to achieve the RM1 billion earnings milestone.
On the face of it, companies having such strong financial performance should not be trading at 5 sen. That is the paradox facing Zetrix.
Its financials are the not the problem, rather it is a crisis of confidence. For Zetrix, restoring confidence in the company is paramount.

Under Wong’s leadership, the group realised its e-government services business model was inherently risky as the need for such a “middleman” was untenable in the long run. The expansion of the MyJPJ app signals the government is increasingly capable of providing digital services directly.

Its name change last year to Zetrix from My EG is a reflection of its strategy of transforming itself from an e-government services provider into a blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) company.

Its robust financial performance in recent years can be attributed to this transformation. Blockchain and AI-related revenue increased from RM127.6 million in 2023 to RM362.8 million in 2024, and RM643.5 million in 2025.

Its first half FY2026 earnings of over half a billion ringgit was supported by AI subscriptions and services, Web3 application fees and sales of Zetrix Layer-1 nodes. Nevertheless, non-AI and non-blockchain activities still account for about 40% of group revenue.
However, this transformation seems to have become its achilles heels as it has racked up huge debt to roll out the new business.
By end-June 2026, cumulative development expenditure had reached a whopping RM3.7 billion from RM2.85 billion at end-2025. That expenditure is likely to continue growing.

At end-June, Zetrix had RM541.6 million in cash and cash equivalents against RM853.1 million in short-term loans and borrowings. Total borrowings stood at RM2.2 billion, up 74.3% from RM1.26 billion a year earlier.

Its current financial woes may well be linked to the burgeoning debt to finance its investment in blockchain infrastructure, AI applications and international expansion. The question remains whether Zetrix has bitten off more than it can chew?

While the transformation appears to be bearing fruit with rising revenue and earnings, investors and financial institutions want to know if these are recurring and sustainable, given the huge investment involved.
Last throw of the dice

Zetrix may have a trump card to deal with its rising debt and cashflow issues as it is preparing to list its AI and blockchain unit, AI Foundation Lab, on the Nasdaq by end-2026. The plan is even backed by a US$40 million (RM163 million) equity investment from International Finance Corp, the World Bank’s investment arm.

The company is targeting a valuation of US$3 billion (RM12.2 billion) alongside a US$200 million (RM816.3 million) capital-raising exercise before the listing, according to a CLSA note. It plans to eventually pare down its stake in the US-listed company, with proceeds to be used to reduce its debt, and potentially pay a special dividend.

However, these projections were done prior to the brutal selloff, which has thrown a spanner into the works. MARC said its proposed Nasdaq listing could be deferred to the first quarter of 2027 from its initial end-2026 target.
“While the proposed listing could broaden the group’s access to capital, recent developments affecting its business and financial profile could present challenges to its completion,” it said.
It added Zetrix’s reliance on “transactions that remain subject to execution risks” offered limited assurance that funds would be available in time for debt repayment.
This potential Nasdaq listing may well be the last throw of the dice for Wong and Zetrix. If it is executed successfully, they may well be able to prevent the company from falling off the precipice.

ab004f619c0b5081: The renminbi is back at the centre of debates about global macroeconomic imbalances. With China’s merchandise trade surplus widening to US$1.2 trillion in 2025, and with its manufacturing sector becoming increasingly dominant, the near-consensus among financial and economic commentators is that the renminbi is significantly undervalued.

The implication is that China should let its currency appreciate sharply, thereby shrinking its surplus, easing competitive pressure on manufacturers elsewhere, and helping rebalance the global economy.

This argument is politically convenient, because it points to a seemingly painless solution. Unfortunately, it suffers from a fatal flaw. Before simply assuming that exchange-rate appreciation is appropriate for China, one must examine the underlying cause of the currency’s weakness.

If it was primarily the result of deliberate interventions to expand exports, rapid appreciation would indeed be a relatively clean remedy. But if it reflects weak domestic demand, allowing the currency to appreciate without addressing the underlying weakness would be counterproductive.
China falls into the second category. The renminbi’s weakness and the widening surplus are better understood as parallel consequences of a deep adjustment in the real-estate sector.

Property was once a central engine of Chinese demand, credit creation, local-government finance, household wealth, and investment. When the property market suffers, so does domestic demand, particularly investment demand. And when investment falls faster than national saving, the external surplus rises.

China is not unusual in this respect. CF40 Research has identified a clear pattern: housing busts have improved economies’ external balances. That is what happened previously in the US and Japan, where weak domestic demand also led to persistently low inflation.

While the renminbi’s nominal exchange rate has been quite stable against both the US dollar and a basket of currencies in recent years, high global inflation and low domestic inflation have produced a large real depreciation. It is not a weak currency that has undermined domestic demand and led to large external surpluses; it is the opposite.

The renminbi’s exchange rate matters, but how it adjusts matters more. An appreciation driven by an economic recovery would be welcome. If the property sector stabilises, household confidence improves, productive investment rises, and imports grow, the currency would strengthen as part of the broader rebalancing.

But too abrupt an appreciation would not repair China’s property market or revive domestic demand. On the contrary, it would hurt the export sector and the investment and consumption that it supports.
The impact on global imbalances would be ambiguous, but it would almost certainly slow China’s recovery, potentially leading to weaker growth for a world economy that would be no less unbalanced.

The rest of the world therefore has a big stake in how China adjusts. China has become a price anchor for a large part of global manufacturing, since producer prices increasingly shape goods prices elsewhere, even when the final product is not imported directly from China.

In fact, weak Chinese demand and a low renminbi exchange rate have helped restrain goods inflation in advanced economies, though this benefit receives far less attention than the competitive pressure China places on foreign producers.

The post-Covid disinflation in advanced economies was a case in point. It came not only from tighter monetary policies and repaired supply chains, but also from soft Chinese manufactured-goods prices.
Sharp currency appreciation would push in the opposite direction, raising the price of Chinese exports. The result would feel less like a painless rebalancing than a cost-push shock.

Such an adjustment would not promote factory construction in Europe, higher productivity in the US, or improvements in China’s property market. It would simply increase the global prices of manufactured goods at a time when inflation in many advanced economies remains elevated. Some foreign producers might welcome the easing of Chinese competition, but central banks’ job would get harder.

Bond markets would also feel the effects. Expectations of higher inflation and tighter monetary policy would increase pressure on nominal yields at a time when advanced economies are already drawing down global savings.

With the US running large fiscal deficits, Europe preparing for more spending on defense and infrastructure, and AI investments creating enormous demand for capital, the need for savings from the rest of the world has grown.

In this context, one must remember that China’s surplus is the counterpart of Chinese net savings supplied to the rest of the world. If China absorbs more at home, less Chinese savings will be available to finance deficits abroad.
That could drive a healthy adjustment if deficit countries were to save more and borrow less. But failing that, bond yields—which have already climbed to multi-year highs—must continue to rise.
None of this means that China should hold down its currency artificially. Rather, it should try to rebalance by strengthening domestic demand.
That means stabilising the property sector, improving household income expectations, expanding social insurance, and shifting investment towards more productive uses.
Such policies would narrow the surplus more durably than exchange-rate adjustment alone. The renminbi would duly strengthen as the recovery takes hold.

But deficit countries have responsibilities, too. They cannot demand smaller Chinese surpluses while continuing to count on cheap imported goods, disinflationary pressure, and abundant foreign savings. If advanced economies want China to absorb more of what it produces, they must show more fiscal discipline themselves.
Kai Guo is executive president and senior fellow of the CF40 Institute.

dcfb53d029e382f8: Last week it was Atletico Madrid and Lisandro Martinez; this week Como and Bruno Fernandes.
Another defeat in Europe, another voice in the dressing room feeling compelled to cry out.
Such insubordination would once have meant instant dismissal even for the stellar likes of Roy Keane and David Beckham.
But today, a geological age of anguish later, almost all fans and probably most players feel the complainant is stating the obvious.
For many of the bedraggled army that still follow United in Europe, the sentiment was not for sacking another manager, but for removing the hierarchy.
You would hope that the richest United fans might resort to a revival of the Red Knights that tried to wrest control of the club in 2010.
Mere millionaires came up short last time, but if billionaires were serious, and fans make life difficult for Ratcliffe, you never know.
Beckham is a billionaire now. In 2010, he wore a green and gold scarf to give his support. He needs to rustle up a few rich cronies.
Club captain Fernandes did bring tactics into it, which are at Michael Carrick’s door, but the loathing for the ownership is ratcheting up several notches.
If losing at Atletico Madrid could not be compared to Grimsby or the recent home loss to Brighton after a two-goal lead, Como is in a league of its own.
As recently as 2019, Como were in Italy’s Serie D playing at a communal stadium with a capacity of just over 1,000.
They are managed by Cesc Fabregas, who is remembered as much for throwing pizza at Sir Alex Ferguson as for his spells in midfield with Arsenal and Chelsea.
At the ‘Battle of the Buffet’, it was just a slice; this was the whole pizza, deep-pan with lots of topping.
Como were all over them and United didn’t deserve even a late consolation.
To have progressed to Europe’s premier competition under a rookie manager in that time is a salutary tale for United. Another one.
In between these losses, United managed a creditable draw at Leeds, but they have won only two of ten games this season.
They are a precarious 21st in the Champions League table.
They’re on course for the second-round playoffs, but not a million miles from the ignominy of elimination (positions 25 to 36).
In the EPL, they are 13th, but play Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa, Arsenal and Liverpool next.
No one is predicting a surge up the table.
We pretty well know what will happen next. Carrick will cling on till December, eking out the odd result.
Jim Ratcliffe will say he’s “fully supportive” while interviewing all the usual suspects.
And so it goes on.
As the fans are all too painfully aware, changing the manager doesn’t work.
With the exception of Tommy Docherty’s five-year reign, United has had only two successful managers since the Second World War.
Matt Busby, appointed in 1945 – delayed while he completed military service – and Fergie in 1986.
Looking at the names post-Fergie, they should have done better. David Moyes is still at it with Everton, having led West Ham to a European trophy.
Louis van Gaal is one of the giants of the era and, despite illness, took the Netherlands to a quarter-final loss on penalties to Argentina in the 2022 World Cup.
He was sacked immediately after winning the FA Cup with United and blames City’s “cheating” for his demise.
Jose Mourinho is now at Real Madrid, but he did win the League Cup and Europa League. United were not that bad in those days.
Ralf Rangnick lasted only months as an interim, but it’s widely accepted that he was “sacked” by Ronaldo.
Where was the hierarchy? Where were the Glazers?
And where were they when Rangnick gave his list of players he wanted United to sign?
Avert your gaze now, United fans, as it could be painful reading. Among them were: Erling Haaland, Luis Diaz, Julian Alvarez, Enzo Fernandez, and Josko Gvardiol.
With those and under his astute guidance – he was mentor to the likes of Jurgen Klopp, Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann – United could have outdone City.
And there are two more. Between the outbursts by Martinez and Fernandes, Erik ten Hag took a swipe as well.
The Dutchman revealed that he’d wanted Harry Kane and Declan Rice, but his request fell on deaf ears.
Fergie had famously said he’d suffered more pain dealing with Spurs chairman Daniel Levy than from his hip operation, so chief executive Richard Arnold and football director John Murtough didn’t try.
Even though Kane was desperate for the move!
Ditto West Ham and Rice. The Hammers didn’t want to sell, but Arsenal managed to prise their star asset away a year later for £110m.
With those seven players, United would have had a side to take on the world.
Ten Hag also partly blames City for his sacking, but in the period of City’s illegal £900m spending spree, United matched them almost pound for pound, totally above board.
But the Glazers surpassed that figure, taking out an estimated £1.5 billion in dividends and interest.
Absentee owners, incompetent directors. Enter Ratcliffe and the Politburo.
Where the Glazers treat United as a cash cow, to Ratcliffe it’s a hobby horse.
The billionaire sports fan loves to dabble in several and involves his petrochemical company, INEOS.
But unfortunately for him and his many victims, he has the Sadim touch – the opposite of Midas. Or, what has been dubbed the INEOS Curse.
In football, French club Nice have had seven managers in five years while Swiss club Lausanne suffered relegation before coming back up.
The dominant SKY cycling team lost their way when INEOS took over, as did Mercedes in F1 as soon as INEOS sponsorship came in.
Britain’s America's Cup sailing challenge ended in humiliation and litigation after Ratcliffe took over.
Even the mighty All Blacks suddenly became vulnerable with Ratcliffe’s backing.
Cash cow or hobby horse? Between them, the owners have cooked up a real dog’s breakfast.
It’s time for the Red Knights to ride again.

4a7fb2460297143f: A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."

The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.

Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read-and-write access to portions of system memory.
